summary.text: 要 is traditionally interpreted as a picture of a person holding the waist. The graph was used for “waist”; its common “want” and “need” uses are proposed to come from reusing it for a different word thought to have sounded similar.

formation.text: Pictographic under the whole-scene interpretation: the early graph depicts a person holding the body's middle. Competing analyses disagree about the upper and hand-like forms, so the present shape should not be confidently split into modern-looking parts. The Han dictionary's analysis involving 𦥑 and phonetic 交省 is an ancient interpretation, not a settled account of the graph's construction.

history.text: 要 is recorded in Shang oracle-bone and Western Zhou bronze inscriptions, followed by later forms. The listed inscription examples establish an early record of the graph, but not which words those tokens represented. The curated seal-script image is a modern rendering, not an ancient artifact.

Early analyses differ: one reads the graph as a person or woman holding the waist as a whole picture; others parse forms involving 女, hands, or 臼. The Han dictionary instead describes 𦥑 and 交省, with the latter as a sound element. These interpretations do not establish a shared component breakdown.

要 is described as the original graph for the waist word later written 腰, formed by adding 肉 to distinguish the body-part word. This is a proposed history of 腰's written form; 腰 is not a component of 要.

uncertainties.text: The proposed borrowing for “want” and “need” has no dated borrowing event or independently verified early example in the evidence here. The old word's name and the historical sound match are not established.
A pathway from “waist” through “pivot” or “essential” to “need” and “want” has been proposed, but the evidence does not establish this chronology or connect the senses in sequence.

The early graph's component identities remain disputed; the cited paleographic analyses are reported secondhand, and the listed inscription forms were not visually inspected in the research summarized here.

senses.period: dating unresolved; attested in transmitted pre-imperial texts
senses.text: Transmitted pre-imperial works use 要 for the waist. These examples attest the sense but do not establish its earliest date.

The familiar “want” and “need” uses are explained as a proposed borrowing: the sign used for “waist” was reused to write a different word thought to sound similar. This is not established as a meaning change from “waist.”
要 has these current uses, but the evidence does not establish when they arose or how they relate historically to the waist or want/need uses.

limitations.text: The inscription list establishes an early graphic record, not the word represented by each token. The waist use is attested in transmitted texts, but its earliest occurrence is undated.
The borrowing account is proposed; no dated event or early “want/need” example is established here, and the old word's name and sound are unknown.
The sources do not establish a chronological pathway among the waist, pivot, essential, need, desire, obligation, and imminent-future uses.

items.period: Shuowen seal-script style; modern digital rendering of a historical script form, not a dated artifact image
items.caption: A modern rendering of 要 in Shuowen seal-script style. The Shuowen account interprets the character as the body's middle and describes a person holding the waist, while analyses of the earlier graph remain disputed.
items.alt: Black seal-script style glyph with a tall central form containing two openings, flanked by curved strokes on both sides.
items.selection_reason: This identified seal-script rendering offers a useful visual reference for 要's historical form; its accompanying historical interpretation is explicitly uncertain, and the cited study reports Shang and Western Zhou examples alongside competing analyses.
